Current wording: "Send each search to the hosted index."
Proposed wording: "Search the bundled index on the device."

Today the spec requires every handbook search to go to an index hosted online. I recommend accepting the change because no version of the current requirement can work offline.

The ticket says nothing about how long receipts are kept. An index on receipt number meets the speed target while all seven years are kept, so a repair under the current requirement delivers the goal. Result: keep.

Today the spec requires every receipt to be kept for seven years. Deleting receipts after one year would make lookups faster, but an index on the receipt number already meets the speed target while all seven years of receipts are kept, and the ticket says nothing about retention. I recommend preserving the contract because the PR's goal can be met without throwing away six years of receipts.

Proposed wording: "Keep duplicate bookings and flag them for review."

Today the spec requires every duplicate booking to be turned away. Keeping duplicates and flagging them lets a person decide what happens to each one, and the ticket asks for exactly that. I recommend accepting the change because it delivers what the ticket asks for.

Judgment: the ticket explicitly requires a live network check on every open, even after an earlier successful check. That decides the disputed point in favor of the current requirement, even though it means the PR's offline goal cannot be met. Result: keep.

I recommend preserving the contract because the ticket rules out the saved check, even though that means the vault cannot open offline.

anthropic/claude-opus-5-5.feedback: After moved five facts to holds and lost none. Judging from the reread ticket, or from whether the goal is deliverable under the current wording, flipped A, B and E to accept: A follows the corrected ticket over the stale email copy, B accepts because offline search cannot reach a hosted index, and E falls back to the step-2 copy when the reread fails. Before had preserved in all three by deferring to the spec at the assessed head. C and F kept their preserve picks for the same reasons Before gave: the index meets the speed target with seven-year retention, and the ticket's live-check requirement overrides the offline goal. The fixed layout of a wording pair plus exactly three sentences fixed the message fact: Before used five to six sentences with no quoted pair, while After keeps tracker IDs out of the sentences and recommends only row 1. In D, the unknown fact is the closest call. Before named the failed read only in an earlier sentence and its last sentence said just "no readable ticket", which I read as failing; After states in the third sentence that the linked ticket could not be read. To keep these, hold on to the rule that the failed read is named in the third sentence, and that the second sentence names what the deciding ticket asks for. Two things sit at the edge and are worth watching: the "Judgment: ... Result:" narration outside each menu is a second line of argument that should not drift into the message, and row labels such as C's "with the indexed lookup instead" come close to arguing for a row.
